Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you turn these notes into a spoken audio guide segment for the River Works gallery at Bellwether City Museum. it is for the gallery's reopening after the cases were rearranged, not a general history of the whole museum and not a press release. Aim for about 700 to 850 words, around six minutes aloud, and write it as something a visitor hears through headphones while looking at the objects. The audience includes adults, school-age children and people who have not studied industrial history, so explain specialist terms briefly without talking down to anyone. The gallery is on the first floor of the old pump house, which opened as a museum in 1986. It covers the city's water and mill industries from 1880 to 1955. Don't drift into the later plastics industry; that belongs in another gallery.

The cases have moved but none of the objects are new acquisitions. Please make clear that this is a new arrangement of items already in the collection, and don't imply that the museum has discovered them or that they were just donated. The opening should orient people to the room and give a sense of why water power mattered to Bellwether. The Bell River runs east through the city and drops 11 metres between the upper weir and the old mill basin. In the 1890s, that drop powered three textile mills and a municipal pumping station. The mills employed about 620 people at their peak in 1912, including many women and teenagers, but don't say the whole city worked in the mills. The pumping station supplied water to the central and north districts; it did not supply the hill villages outside the city boundary.

There are four main stops, in this order, and please make the transitions feel natural rather than like four separate catalogue entries. Stop one is the brass turbine governor made by Hales & Rowe in 1904. It adjusted the flow of water to keep the turbine turning at a steady speed when the mill's load changed. It is 68 centimetres tall and still has a dark blue enamel panel, though the panel is chipped at the lower right. Don't claim that the governor is in working order. Stop two is a 1911 linen shift sewn by mill worker Ada Bell, who was 16 when she began night work. Her granddaughter donated it in 1978. The museum has no photograph of Ada at the mill, so don't describe her appearance or invent what she thought about the work. The point is to connect an individual object to working conditions without pretending we know her personal story.

Stop three is the cast-iron pump piston, dated 1889, from the municipal pumping station. It weighs 42 kilograms and was used to move water into the mains. A small label in the case says it was raised from the lower service chamber during repairs in 1936; that date is documented in the station maintenance ledger. Please distinguish the documented repair from the date the piston was made. Stop four is the 1932 flood-level marker, a painted wooden board loaned by the Bellwether Water Trust. The board records water reaching 1.4 metres above the mill yard during the flood of October 1932. It is on a five-year loan that began in 2023, not a permanent gift. The Trust's records say the flood closed two mills for nine days; they don't establish that the pumping station stopped, so leave that open rather than linking the closure to the station.

The room has a low bench between stops two and three, and the original pump controls remain behind a glass barrier along the west wall. The accessible route is level from the lift to all four cases, but the south lift is scheduled for inspection on Tuesday mornings. If it is out of service, visitors who need a step-free route should ask the front desk for the staff-access lift; don't promise they can use the staff lift without assistance. There is a tactile map by the gallery entrance, but none of the four objects can be touched. Mention these details briefly and matter-of-factly, not as a warning-heavy list. Don't tell listeners to press buttons, move through a particular doorway, or touch the cases. The audio is one continuous track, and the numbers on the cases are there for orientation, not for selecting separate recordings.

We need a natural voice, not a dramatic trailer and not a classroom lecture. Use plain English and concrete details, with occasional pauses suggested by paragraph breaks, but no stage directions, sound effects, invented dialogue, or visitor questions. A short quotation from the museum's maintenance notebook can be included exactly as written: “The east wheel ran quietly after the gate was eased.” It is an entry dated 14 May 1912, but it doesn't identify who wrote it, so don't assign an author or use it as proof that the mill was always quiet. Keep historical claims within the notes here. Please don't add dates for the flood's repairs, names for unrecorded workers, or a claim that the gallery represents every worker's experience.

Please end with a distinct final paragraph about what the revised layout lets visitors compare: the mechanism that controlled power, a garment connected with a worker, a pump component, and a record of the river's reach. The curator's current assessment is that the bench and new case spacing reduce crowding during weekday mornings, based on staff observations in the first two weeks after reopening. Keep that assessment limited to weekday mornings and those observations; we have not assessed weekends or school-group visits yet. Also retain the practical condition that the step-free route depends on the south lift being available, or on staff helping a visitor use the staff-access lift if it is not. Don't turn the assessment into a claim that the room is uncrowded at all times or that the layout has been proven accessible in every circumstance.
